extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy (Aristotle / virtue ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and characterizing moral states and virtues according to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (Books IV–V), including the doctrine of the mean and the different species of justice. Focus is on identifying praiseworthy mean states and their opposed excesses/defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean state is praiseworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state is praiseworthy, in virtue of which we are angry with those with whom, and at those things with which, we ought to be angry, and in right manner; excesses and defects are blameable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess and deficiency are blameable to degrees (slightly if only slight, more so if greater, very blameable when considerable). The decision about what degree or kind of transgression is blameable rests with the Moral Sense and must be judged in particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral judgement rests on particulars / Moral Sense
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not easy to lay down, in so many words, for what degree or kind of transgression a man is blameable: because the decision is in particulars, and rests therefore with the Moral Sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rules point to the mean, but application requires sensitivity to context, particular persons, and circumstances rather than rigid formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of social intercourse by propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: Social intercourse should be regulated by propriety: the aim is to avoid giving pain and to contribute to pleasure, but with a constant reference to what is noble and expedient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should prefer to give pleasure and avoid pain generally, but if contributing to pleasure is dishonourable or hurtful, or unseemly to the doer, one should prefer to give pain or oppose. Differences among people (great men vs ordinary men, intimates vs strangers) require adjusting behaviour 'giving to each his due.' One may inflict trifling pain with a view to consequent pleasure when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean between Over-Complaisant and Cross/Contentious (amiable/appropriate friendliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who always agree to give pleasure are Over-Complaisant; those who oppose everything are Cross and Contentious; the mean is a state most like Friendship — amiable, earnest, independent of special affection, doing what is proper alike to intimates and strangers as propriety requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mean-person acts from natural disposition to do what is proper, not from love or hatred, and tailors behaviour to the relationship and context (not treating intimates and strangers alike). Motive matters: doing agreeable acts for profit is Flattery rather than pure complaisance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of motives in social behaviour (flatterer vs disinterested complaisance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who seeks to give pleasure simply and disinterestedly is Over-Complaisant; if he does so to secure profit (wealth or its goods) he is a Flatterer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motives affect blameworthiness: similar outward acts can be morally different depending on whether they are done for profit, honour, or disinterested amiability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness as a mean between Exaggeration and Reserve
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean character is Plain-matter-of-fact and Truthful: admitting what really belongs to him and making it neither greater nor less than the truth. The Exaggerator overclaims credit; the Reserved man depreciates his own qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Falsehood is low and blameable; truth is noble and praiseworthy. Exaggeration is especially blameable. Reserve may appear refined and have some virtues when used moderately and where truth is not obvious, but excessive reserve can resemble exaggeration; motives (pleasure in falsehood vs motive for gain or glory) change the moral evaluation (braggart vs liar for gain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of boasting/exaggeration by motive (braggart vs factotum)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man exaggerates without special motive he is base or a fool; if he exaggerates for honour or glory he is a Braggart (less blameworthy); if for pecuniary considerations he is more unseemly. Those who lay false claim to trivial or obvious things are called Factotums and are despicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify falsehoods by underlying motive: love of falsehood for its own sake (liar), desire of glory (braggart), gain (more unseemly). The social perception of refinement may make some reserve seem tasteful, but moral worth still hinges on truth-love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jocularity and the mean (buffoon/vulgar vs clownish/stern; mean = tact/ease)
rubrics_metrics.description: In jocularity there is excess (Buffoons/Vulgar) who catch at the ridiculous at any cost, and defect (Clownish/Stern) who will not joke; the mean is Jocular in good taste, denoted by a Greek term expressing 'ease of movement' (Tact/Easy Pleasantry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buffoons aim merely to raise laughter, sometimes causing pain to the object of wit; the refined jocular person says and listens to what is fit for a gentleman. There is a difference between vulgar and gentlemanly jesting (e.g., obscene Old Comedy vs innuendo in New Comedy). A man will generally do what he will bear to hear, but jesting is a species of scurrility and some points may be rightly forbidden; the refined person is a law to himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tact as a moral quality of jocularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Tact: characteristic of a man of Tact to say and listen to such things as are fit for a good man and a gentleman to say and hear; avoids causing pain and maintains decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tact distinguishes gentlemanly jocularity from vulgarity and from the unproductive clownishness. The refined person endures certain jests but will not tolerate scurrility beyond lawful or decent bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buffoon and Clownish as moral extremes in jocularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Buffoons are those who cannot resist the ridiculous and spare neither themselves nor others to raise a laugh; Clownish persons are useless in such intercourse, contributing nothing jocose and being hostile to those who do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These character-types illustrate excess (buffoon) and deficiency (clownishness) relative to the mean of tact/easy pleasantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shame is a feeling, not a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Shame is more like a feeling than a moral state; defined as 'a kind of fear of disgrace'. It is suitable to youth as a check but not to the mature good man; to be shamefaced as an old man is not praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shame arises at voluntary actions only, and a truly good man ('one that is good in himself') ought not to do disgraceful things, so shame does not count as a virtue. It may be good only on the supposition 'if a man should do such things he would feel Shame.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-control is not properly a virtue but a mixed state
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-Control is not properly a Virtue, but a kind of mixed state; full account to be given in a later book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked as distinct from the virtues discussed here; to be treated separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a moral state enabling one to do and wish the just
rubrics_metrics.description: All men mean by 'Justice' a moral state such that in consequence men have the capacity of doing what is just, actually do it, and wish it; similarly, Injustice is a moral state such that men do unjustly and wish what is unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice is both a mean and has multiple senses (lawful and equal). The inquiry asks what actions are its object-matter and what mean it is. Justice differs from other states because it concerns transactions 'towards one's neighbour.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as perfect virtue in relation to others
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is in fact perfect Virtue, but not simply so — it is perfect as exercised towards one's neighbour. It is thought oftentimes to be the best of the Virtues because it is the practice of perfect Virtue towards others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person may be virtuous privately but inept in dealings with others; justice measures the capacity to practise virtue in community and under rule. Thus 'all virtue is in Justice comprehended' in a certain sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawful (by law) things are in a manner Just
rubrics_metrics.description: The violator of the law is Unjust, and the keeper of the Law Just; all Lawful things are in a manner Just because laws aim (ideally) at common good or some standard of goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws command deeds of various virtues (bravery, self-mastery, meekness) and forbid vices; good law enjoins actions conducive to the social common good. But law-based justice is not the whole of particular justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two species of particular justice: Distributive and Corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular Justice has species: one concerned with distributions of honour, wealth, etc. (distributive), and the other Corrective justice arising in transactions between man and man (corrective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distributive justice is according to proportion (geometrical proportion — equality of ratios); corrective justice aims to restore equality where there has been gain and loss (arithmetical equality between parties). Transactions may be voluntary (selling, buying, bail, etc.) or involuntary (theft, adultery, false witness, violence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive justice = proportionate equality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Just in distributions is the proportionate: persons should receive shares in the same ratio as the relevant rate (e.g., contribution, rank, virtue) — the Just implies four terms A:B :: C:D; distribution is just when it preserves that ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What the 'rate' is (freedom, wealth, nobility of birth, virtue) is contested among political groups. The unjust is what violates the proportionate; distributive justice is a mean relative to disproportionate allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective justice = arithmetic equality (mean between gain and loss)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrective justice arises in transactions and treats parties as previously equal; when an injury causes unequal gain and loss, the judge attempts to restore equality by penalty — the Just is the mean between loss and gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrective justice is not proportionate but arithmetical: equality is restored by taking from the gain and compensating the loss. The judge is conceived as personifying the mean (the Just) and resolves disputes by restoring balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice is a mean and involves equality between persons and things
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Unjust is unequal, the Just is equal, which is a mean between greater and less; the Just implies four terms at least (two persons and two things) and requires that the ratio of persons to persons equals the ratio of things to things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disputes about the proper rate of distribution (who is 'equal' in what respect) are the root of quarrelling; the mathematical notion of proportion underlies distributive justice, whereas corrective justice uses arithmetic equality to correct transactions.
